defendant: S&P Data Ohio, LLC (1500 West Third Street, Cleveland, OH 44113)
agreement: "Grant Agreement" between JobsOhio as Grantor and S&P Data Ohio, LLC as Grantee, for up to $150,000.00 in grant funds "on a reimbursement basis." Amended by an "Amendment to Grant Agreement" on or about June 14, 2018 (Exhibit 2). The complaint calls the two together the "Grant Agreement." The agreement itself is headed "JOBSOHIO GRANT AGREEMENT" and recites that "Grantee will use the financial assistance in accordance with JobsOhio's grant guidelines to invest in workforce training associated with Grantee's project at the Project Address."
agreement_date: The complaint pleads "On or about April 8, 2018" (para. 4), and the September 12, 2023 demand letter also says "dated April 8, 2018." The attached agreement itself states "Effective Date: February 6, 2018." Both dates are read directly from the filing; the complaint and the exhibit do not agree. Amendment to Grant Agreement on or about June 14, 2018.
program: Not named as one of JobsOhio's published programs in the complaint. The attached agreement carries "Program No.: SFPN_2017_441860-WF" in its header grid, and its recital describes the use as "invest in workforce training." No program name appears anywhere in the complaint.
amount_sought: $150,000.00, plus interest including prejudgment interest, reasonable attorney fees, costs and expenses. Notably, JobsOhio's own September 12, 2023 demand letter had demanded only $75,000.00 and said that figure was "non-negotiable." The complaint explains the jump: because the company did not pay the $75,000 within 30 days, "JobsOhio therefore seeks damages in the entire amount of the grant funds provided to Defendant, being $150,000.00" (para. 11).
job_commitments: From the first page of the attached Grant Agreement: No. of Jobs to be Created: 180; Total Payroll to be Created: $6,000,000; No. of Jobs to be Retained: 122; Total Payroll to be Retained: $5,197,754; No. of Employees to be Trained: 225; Total Training Investment: $359,307. Effective Date February 6, 2018; Metric Evaluation Date December 31, 2020; Metric Expiration Date December 31, 2022. Project Site 1500 West Third Street, Cleveland, OH 44113 (Cuyahoga County).
shortfall: Per the company's own 2022 Annual Report, as pleaded at para. 9 and repeated in the demand letter: "Defendant only created 136 new jobs at the Project Site, instead of the required 180 new jobs, and the new jobs had an associated payroll of $4,000,000.00, instead of the required payroll of at least $6,000,000.00." The complaint does not state what happened to the retention, training-headcount or training-investment metrics.

Section 9(a) lists ten Breach triggers, (i) through (x), including "(vii) Grantee admits its inability to pay its debts as such debts become due; (viii) Grantee commences a voluntary bankruptcy; (ix) an involuntary bankruptcy action occurs against Grantee which remains undismissed or unstayed for sixty (60) days; or (x) Grantee has ceased operations at the Project Address for a period greater than ninety (90) consecutive days." Section 9(d): "Remedies Cumulative. No remedy provided to Grantor under this agreement or otherwise by law or in equity is exclusive of any other available remedy." Section 9(e): "Grantor's Expenses. ALSO FROM THE ATTACHED AGREEMENT, the discretion clauses that do not appear in the complaint's block quotes. Section 5(c) ends: "Notwithstanding, Grantor has the discretion to waive non-compliance if, in writing, Grantee submits to Grantor a description of Market Conditions and Other Factors regarding Grantee and its operations at the Project site. notes: The most important finding in this case is that the full executed JobsOhio Grant Agreement is in the public record, attached as Exhibit 1. It is a workforce-training grant on a reimbursement basis, Program No. SFPN_2017_441860-WF. Second finding: the gap between the demand and the suit. JobsOhio demanded $75,000, half the award, and called the figure non-negotiable; when the company did not pay within the 30 days Section 9(b)(ii) allows, JobsOhio sued for the whole $150,000 and took judgment for the whole $150,000. Third: the agreement gives JobsOhio sole discretion both to "determine compliance" (5(a)) and to "waive repayment of all or a portion of the Grant Funds disbursed" (5(c)), on factors it alone weighs. Fourth: the complaint and the attached agreement disagree on the agreement's date, April 8, 2018 versus an Effective Date of February 6, 2018. Grant schedule shows $650,000 paid to this recipient across 2018 and 2021; this suit concerns only a $150,000 agreement, so the other payments were under instruments not in this docket. The company's 2022 Annual Report numbers come to the court only through JobsOhio's pleading; the report itself is not in the record. Two judges appear on the case, Dan Hawkins on the judgment and Richard D Brown on the satisfaction, because of mass courtroom transfers on 12/30/2024 and 01/03/2025 shown on the docket.

notes: This is the second Talent Acquisition Services Agreement in the set, and its Section 9(b)(ii) "Liquidated Damages" text is nearly identical to the one in the Olive AI case, so the TAS form appears to be standard. Three findings stand out. First, JobsOhio sued for the entire $429,750.19 of service value on a reporting failure alone. The complaint pleads no shortfall in jobs or payroll and says the metric breach is only "upon information and belief." Under this contract, not filing a form on March 1 is enough to owe back every dollar JobsOhio spent on subcontractors. Second, the same company also has a separate grant agreement with JobsOhio that the complaint names but excludes from the suit, so one company can hold two different JobsOhio instruments with two different repayment regimes. Third, the agreement is withheld for confidentiality, so Exhibit A, the "Talent Acquisition Services Value Allocation" that decides the dollar figure, is not public and the $429,750.19 cannot be checked against anything. Service of the original complaint failed at the Dublin address on 2024-02-22, "NOT DELIVERABLE AS ADDRESSED," which fits the merger of Nexient into NTT DATA Americas on 2023-01-01, about seven months before JobsOhio sued the dissolved entity. Grant schedule shows $446,530 paid to this recipient in 2020 and 2021, close to but not equal to the $429,750.19 sought.

notes: Two things in this docket matter more than the numbers. First, paragraph 7 of the complaint: JobsOhio tells the court, with a citation, that Ohio law would let it take back all $150,000 for this breach and that it chose to ask for $50,000 instead. That is a public statement of how much discretion sits behind the figure in any of these suits. The case it cites, State of Ohio Dept. of Dev. v. Matrix Centennial, L.L.C., 2014-Ohio-3251, is a state Development Department grant case, not a JobsOhio one, so JobsOhio is borrowing a state agency's authority for its own private contract. Second, the demand letter is the only document in the ten dockets where JobsOhio itself uses the word "clawback," and it uses it to describe a Section 9(b)(ii) repayment demand: "the request for clawback is not the full amount of the disbursed grant funds." Everywhere else the agreements call the same thing "Demand Repayment of Grant Funds." Third, the agreement reached the public record only because JobsOhio noticed, three months later, that its exhibits "inadvertently did not come through" and refiled them. The complaint on its own quotes no repayment provision at all. Fourth, the shortfall is 17 of 42 jobs and the demand was one third of the money, roughly proportionate but never explained as a formula. The demand letter gives the same reasoning JobsOhio gave in every other grant case here, jobs created, jobs retained, fixed assets, market conditions and other factors. The agreement's Section 9 text was not read page by page in this pass; the pages read were the header grid, the recital, Section 1 and the signature page.
